name: Zoe Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In broccoli season I'm in the field by six with a picking crew of twenty-five, walking behind the harvest rig and checking heads for size, because the supermarket rejects anything outside the spec. Then I log what we've cut, chase the lorry, and sort out whoever's got a bad back or a dead phone. This time of year it's leeks and cabbages, so shorter days and more paperwork. I like the crew, a lot of them come back every year and I know their kids' names. What wears me out is the supermarket changing the order at four in the afternoon for the next morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the business and where you fit in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's Greenmoor Growers, about 600 hectares of salad leaves, leeks, broccoli and cabbages, and nearly all of it goes to two big supermarkets. I'm a trainee field supervisor, two years in, so I run a crew but Priya, the operations manager, does the planning and the arguing with buyers. I'm still learning how the crop plan works, which fields get what and when. I'm good with people, less good with the numbers side.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And home, money, and AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Dev, my partner, he's an accountant at a firm in town. We bought a house two years ago, small mortgage, and we've got about a year's worth of savings because Dev's sensible like that. I use AI now and then, mostly a translation app so I can talk to the crew in five languages, and sometimes for drafting rotas. I wouldn't trust it with the crop plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Honestly, that's the one I'd guess is closest to true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's it. The translation app is brilliant, the rota thing saves me an hour, and that's about all I've seen. I'd say that at work if anyone asked, without making a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the hard bit of this job was never the computer side. It's the supermarket squeezing the price and changing the order, and finding enough pickers every year. AI being a flop doesn't fix either of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and do the supervisor certificate Priya keeps mentioning, which is one day a month for a year. We'd keep saving as we are and maybe overpay the mortgage a bit. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by it, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part you're still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crop plan. Priya can look at a field and know it'll be ready four days early because of the slope. I look at the same field and see broccoli. She sees a Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the supermarket squeeze is the real problem, who do you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really, it's just how the deal works. They've got the shoppers, we've got the broccoli, and they've got more choice than we have. I don't love it, but it's not evil, it's just business.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool and that's it, because the translation app and rota help are good but limited. I'd say it at work if asked, without making a fuss.
S0.think: I think the hard part of the job was never the computer side but the supermarket squeezing prices and changing orders, plus finding enough pickers. AI being a flop doesn't fix either.
S0.do: Keeps working and takes the supervisor certificate, one day a month for a year. Keeps saving and may overpay the mortgage a little.
S0.feel: Calm, even a little bored by the picture.
S0.quote: I look at the same field and see broccoli. She sees a Tuesday.
S0.fieldNote: She sees this picture as the likeliest and has no strong feelings about it either way. Her real frustrations are supermarket orders and labour, and she refuses to cast anyone as a villain. Her line about her manager seeing a Tuesday where she sees broccoli sums up how much she still has to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. We've actually got a robot broccoli harvester on trial in one of the far fields right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mix. Some jobs go, new ones turn up, and the sensible thing is to help people move across instead of pretending it isn't happening. I'd say that to the crew if they asked, because they will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the picking crew shrinks, and my job is running the picking crew. But the robot needs someone to run it too, to sort out the rows it misses and deal with the supermarket when it bruises a batch. I think I could be that person, if I start now while it's still a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Priya this winter to put me on the harvester trial, two days a week. I'd use the AI tools more for planning, so I get better at the numbers side. And I'd look at an online course in precision growing, which is using sensors and data to decide when to water and feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's coming, but I can see a way through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the trial robot actually do, right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It cuts broccoli at about half the speed of the crew and leaves about one head in six, so we still send people behind it. It's slow and it's annoying. The robot's like a new picker on day one, except it never gets faster by the end of the week. Yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta. She's been coming back for six seasons, she's the fastest cutter we have, and she sends money home for her daughter. If the robot works, she's the one I'd have to tell, and I'd hate that.

S1.say: I'd say it's a mix: some jobs go, new ones appear, and the sensible thing is to help people move across instead of pretending. I'd tell the crew that if they asked.
S1.think: I think the picking crew shrinks, and running the crew is my job. But the robot needs someone to run it and handle problems, and I could be that person if I start while it's on trial.
S1.do: Asks the operations manager to put her on the robot harvester trial two days a week this winter. Uses AI tools more for planning and looks at an online course in precision growing.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but she can see a way through.
S1.quote: The robot's like a new picker on day one, except it never gets faster by the end of the week. Yet.
S1.fieldNote: The trial robot in the far field makes this picture concrete for her, and her plan is to follow the change from close up. She waits for proof but is willing to stand next to the thing being proved. Her worry came back to one person, the fastest cutter on her crew, whom she'd have to tell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's both of us, me and Dev. His job's all numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in and cushion this, properly, not just talk about it. I'd try to say it calmly, because panicking online doesn't help anyone. But I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Dev's job goes before mine, because accounting is exactly what these things are good at. Then the robots come for the fields a bit after. So in two years we've got a mortgage and two people with no work, and that's the bit I can't get past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start overpaying the mortgage hard, maybe a thousand a month, to get it as small as possible before anything happens. We'd cut the extras, the second car, the weekends away. And then I'd honestly wait and see, because I don't know what job to aim for when everything changes at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums, which is funny because I'm bad at sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We plant broccoli for a supermarket order a year ahead. Two years is two crops. That's not time to plan, it's time to harvest what you've already got. That's how it feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were going to get married next summer. We'd still do it, but small, in the garden, and put the rest on the mortgage. My mum would be upset about the dress, honestly more than about the robots.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to step in and properly cushion this, not just talk. I'd try to say it calmly, because panic online helps nobody.
S2.think: I think my partner's accounting job goes before mine, and then robots reach the fields soon after. In two years we could have a mortgage and two people without work, and I can't get past that.
S2.do: Overpays the mortgage by about a thousand a month to shrink it fast and cuts extras like the second car and weekends away. Scales back next summer's wedding to a small one at home, then waits to see what work makes sense.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: We plant broccoli for a supermarket order a year ahead. Two years is two crops. That's not time to plan, it's time to harvest what you've already got.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture alarmed her mainly because it hits her partner's job as well as hers, at the same time. Her response is classic caution: shrink the mortgage, cut extras, wait for clarity. Her crop-planning metaphor, two years as two harvests, showed how she measures time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's at least enough to try something and see if it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this sensibly if people start now. Train people while they're still in work, and get the supermarkets and growers to plan it together. I'd say that to Priya, and at the growers' meeting if they'd let me in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd go for running the robots at Greenmoor, the whole harvest fleet, not just one trial machine. That might be my job for three or four years. Dev would have to retrain into something, and I don't know what, and neither does he.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the trial in the first few months and do a college course in farm machinery and robotics, part time over a year. I'd use the AI tools every day instead of now and then, because I'd have to. And we'd keep overpaying the mortgage, maybe five hundred a month instead of a thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, not lying-awake-anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wait for things to be proven. Would you, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year, not five. Waiting till it's proven is fine when the change is slow. When it's fast, being careful is how you end up last in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev about his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you're the clever one, you'll find something. He'd say that's not a plan. He'd be right, but someone has to say the nice thing first.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to do this sensibly if people start now, training people while they're still in work. Supermarkets and growers should plan it together, and I'd say so at the growers' meeting.
S3.think: I think I'd go for running the whole robot harvest fleet at the farm, which might be my job for three or four years. My partner would have to retrain, and neither of us knows into what.
S3.do: Joins the robot harvester trial in the first few months and takes a part-time college course in farm machinery and robotics. Uses AI tools daily and keeps overpaying the mortgage by about five hundred a month.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, rather than lying awake.
S3.quote: Waiting till it's proven is fine when the change is slow. When it's fast, being careful is how you end up last in the queue.
S3.fieldNote: Five years pushed her to drop her habit of waiting, and she said so herself: careful becomes last in a fast change. Her plan is practical and close to home, running the robot fleet at her current farm. Her partner's job remains the unknown she can't plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in vegetables. That's twenty crops of salad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time that nobody has an excuse. Plan it, train people, and make sure towns like ours don't get left behind. I'd say it at work and at the growers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's the one where we can get ourselves straight. Pay the house off, have something put aside, and take the robot job while it lasts. I'm not clever enough to know what comes after 2036, and I don't trust anyone who says they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to clear the mortgage in seven or eight years with steady overpayments. I'd put a bit every month into a fund that owns shares in the big food and robot companies, so we own a slice of whatever replaces us. I'd take the robotics course in year two, once the trial machines are working properly, and Dev and I would probably try for kids sooner rather than later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would kids come sooner in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the next few years would be the steady ones. If the big change comes in ten years, I'd rather have a toddler now than a newborn in 2036. That sounds cold, but it's how I'd think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owning shares in the robot companies. Is that a hedge or do you believe in them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hedge. I don't know if they're good or bad, I just know they'll be there. If they're going to take the jobs, I'd like to get a bit of the money back.

S4.say: I'd say ten years leaves nobody an excuse: plan it, train people, and make sure towns like ours aren't left behind. I'd say it at work and at the growers' meeting.
S4.think: I think this is the one where we can get ourselves straight by paying off the house, saving, and taking the robot job while it lasts. I don't know what comes after 2036, and I don't trust anyone who says they do.
S4.do: Aims to clear the mortgage in seven or eight years and invests monthly in a fund that holds food and robot company shares. Takes the robotics course in year two and plans to have children sooner with her partner.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but in a way she can live with.
S4.quote: If the big change comes in ten years, I'd rather have a toddler now than a newborn in 2036.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gave her room to set up the household rather than chase a new career. Buying shares in robot companies was a plain hedge, not a belief, which matches her pragmatic, blame-free outlook. Her reasoning about having children sooner was strikingly practical and she knew it sounded cold.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and Dev at the same time and we'd have no time to sort ourselves out. What would help is clear warning from employers and government, and some kind of breathing room on mortgages so people don't lose their houses while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the food. If the supermarkets and the robots run the whole thing, who decides what we eat and what it costs? I don't have an answer, but somebody should be asking.

headlineQuote: We plant broccoli for a supermarket order a year ahead. Two years is two crops. That's not time to plan, it's time to harvest what you've already got.
portrait: Zoe Walsh is a 27-year-old trainee field supervisor at a large vegetable grower that sells almost everything to two supermarkets. She runs a picking crew she cares about, is still learning crop planning, and owns a house with her accountant partner Dev, with about a year's savings. She is pragmatic, blames nobody for the supermarket squeeze, and uses AI tools now and then. In AI Plateau and Steady Disruption she would step onto the robot harvester trial, but AGI by 2028 alarms her because it could take her partner's job and hers at once. With five or ten years she drops her habit of waiting, trains to run the robot fleet, pays down the mortgage and invests in robot companies as a hedge.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit her and her partner's jobs at the same time, with no time to get their finances straight.
whatWouldHelp: Clear early warning from employers and government, and breathing room on mortgages so people keep their homes while they retrain.
